The cut inside a column

Doric · square and compass. Chosen groove width 100 mm. Tool at 50% of the arc. Ionic fillets 20% of each pitch (a modern choice). All drawings preserve equal horizontal and vertical scales.

Doric square-and-compass construction: depth = width × (√2 − 1) / 2; edge angle 135°. Ionic semicircle: depth = width / 2; edge angle 90°. The Doric flat-faced alternative has no hollow. Prescriptions do not establish that all surviving ancient profiles follow these curves.

Save the exact coordinates and all three comparisons (CSV). Save the millimetre template (SVG). Print at actual size and check the 25 mm bar; physical printer scaling has not been tested.

Same chord. Which segment?

The green region contains the selected point. The orange arc faces it. A quarter-circle hollow puts P in the smaller segment, making 135°, while Q in the larger segment makes 45°. These are modern degree calculations of the chosen model, not ancient measured flute profiles.

Two isosceles triangles explain P.

CA, CP and CB are radii of one circle. In triangles CAP and CPB, the two base angles in each triangle are equal. Their angles at C divide the cut’s 90° arc.

(180° − 45.00°) ÷ 2 = 67.50°base angle in CAP

(180° − 45.00°) ÷ 2 = 67.50°base angle in CPB

At P, add them: 67.50° + 67.50° = 135°. Moving P changes the two parts but not their sum: 180° − 90° ÷ 2.

A, P, B and Q form a cyclic quadrilateral. Its opposite angles add to two right angles (Euclid III.22), so Q makes 180° − 135° = 45°.

The arc extents and degree arithmetic are modern annotations. A 270° label describes an arc; it does not assign Euclid an ordinary 270° central angle. The Q comparison is geometry, not another carved-flute prescription. Connecting these texts is our teaching choice; it does not document a mason’s method.

Save the exact P/Q comparison on both arcs (CSV).

Read the region and the comparison.

Ἐν κύκλῳ ἡ μὲν ἐν τῷ ἡμικυκλίῳ γωνία ὀρθή ἐστιν, ἡ δὲ ἐν τῷ μείζονι τμήματι ἐλάττων ὀρθῆς, ἡ δὲ ἐν τῷ ἐλάττονι τμήματι μείζων ὀρθῆς

In circulo angulus in semicirculo positus rectus est, qui autem in segmento maiore positus est, minor recto, qui autem in segmento minore positus est, maior recto

“In a circle, the angle in the semicircle is right; that in the larger segment is less than a right angle, and that in the smaller segment is greater than a right angle.”

Euclid III.31, opening comparisons. Greek edited by J. L. Heiberg; Latin translated by Heiberg (1883), not an ancient Latin version. The English and our degree calculations are new. Inspect the Greek page · Inspect the Latin page.

ἐν τῷ μείζονι τμήματι

“In the larger segment.” The dative follows ἐν. τμῆμα → τμήματι names the circular region bounded by a chord and an arc. It is not just the straight line A–B.

ἐλάττων ὀρθῆς

“Less than a right [angle].” ἐλάττων describes the understood γωνία; ὀρθῆς is genitive after the comparison. The larger region contains the smaller angle.

minor recto

Latin makes the same comparison with an ablative: “less than a right [angle].” positus, “placed,” agrees with masculine angulus. in segmento maiore places it in the larger region.

The complete printed sentence continues with the angle of a segment: Greek τοῦ… τμήματος γωνία, Latin angulus segmenti. That later statement concerns an angle made with the curved boundary. Here we measure the straight-chord angle in the segment; the two phrases are not interchangeable. Compare definitions III.6–8.

Read the instructions

A compass and a carpenter’s square.

Doric · IV.3.9

in medio autem quadrato circini centrum conlocetur et agatur linea rotundationis, quae quadrationis angulos tangat

“In the middle of the square let the compass’s centre be placed, and let a curved line be drawn which touches the square’s corners.”

The circle passes through all four corners. Its centre lies half a groove width above the mouth of the cut; the hollow uses a quarter of that circle. Vitruvius also permits twenty flat faces in this paragraph.

Read the Latin construction

in medio quadrato: “in the middle of the square,” with the ablative after in. circini is genitive: “of the compass.” centrum is the subject of the passive command conlocetur, “let it be placed.”

agatur: “let [a line] be drawn.” quae refers back to linea; angulos is what that line touches. The quoted clause avoids the disputed bracketed word earlier in Krohn’s paragraph.

Inspect the complete Latin page

Ionic · III.5.14

cacumenque normae circum rotundationem tangendo pervagari possit

“And the point of the square should be able to travel round the curve, keeping contact.”

The preceding words place the tool against the groove’s corners. With a 90° square, simultaneous contact with both edges is consistent with a semicircular hollow. This paragraph specifies twenty-four flutes.

Read the Latin and its editorial supply

normae means “of the square,” a carpenter’s right-angle tool. cacumen is its point; pervagari possit means “should be able to move about.” tangendo expresses the action of keeping contact.

Krohn prints anconibus 〈angulos〉 striarum dextra ac sinistra tangat: “[it] should touch the groove’s corners on the right and left with its arms.” The brackets mark angulos as an editorial supplement; the apparatus credits Jocundus. Inspect the apparatus beneath the text.

Inspect the Latin and brackets

A Greek word in its own context

The fluting of a column.

ἡ γὰρ τῶν λίθων σύνθεσις ἑτέρα τῆς τοῦ κίονος ῥαβδώσεως

“For the assembling of stones is different from the fluting of a column.”

Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X.4, 1174a23–24. He contrasts different activities within building. This is evidence for the word and its use, not an instruction for carving a profile.

τῆς (τοῦ κίονος) ῥαβδώσεωςof the fluting of the column

κίων → κίονος

“Column,” then “of a column.” The genitive τοῦ κίονος sits inside the larger noun phrase. Its article is masculine.

ῥάβδωσις → ῥαβδώσεως

“Fluting,” then “of fluting.” The feminine article τῆς belongs to this outer noun, not to κίονος. Read the LSJ entry.

ἑτέρα τῆς…

“Different from…” takes the genitive here. σύνθεσις, “assembling,” is the subject; τῶν λίθων tells us what is assembled: stones.
